routes.label: Change base and use one parameter
Express all four values using one logarithm

question: The graphs of \(y=\log_3 x,\) \(y=\log_x 3,\) \(y=\log_{\frac{1}{3}} x,\) and \(y=\log_x\dfrac{1}{3}\) are plotted on the same set of axes. How many points in the plane with positive \(x\)-coordinates lie on two or more of the graphs?
solution:
First separate the domains. The two constant-base logarithms are defined for every \(x>0\). The two logarithms with base \(x\) additionally require \(x\ne1\). At \(x=1\), the constant-base graphs both contain \((1,0)\), giving one intersection point.

For the remaining inputs, let
\[
t=\log_3 x,\qquad t\ne0.
\]
Changing base expresses the four graph values as
\[
t,\qquad \frac1t,\qquad -t,\qquad -\frac1t,
\]
respectively. This makes all possible pairwise equalities simple to check.

The values \(t\) and \(-t\) cannot agree when \(t\ne0\), and neither can \(1/t\) and \(-1/t\). Any other equality compares one of \(t,-t\) with one of \(1/t,-1/t\). Multiplying by the nonzero \(t\) gives either
\[
t^2=1\quad\text{or}\quad t^2=-1.
\]
The second equation has no real solutions, while the first gives \(t=1\) or \(t=-1\).

For \(t=1\), we have \(x=3\), and the values are \(1,1,-1,-1\). This gives \((3,1)\) and \((3,-1)\). For \(t=-1\), we have \(x=1/3\), giving \((1/3,1)\) and \((1/3,-1)\).

These four points are distinct, and none equals \((1,0)\). All pairs of graphs have been covered, so the total is \(\boxed{5}\), choice \(\text{D}\).
